name: Fail Fast and Error Handling Strategies
intent: Make a failure visible at the point where it happens, and decide on purpose, for each kind of error, whether to stop, retry, set the item aside or hand the error to a caller that knows what to do with it.
scenario: A nightly job processes 100 records. Ten are permanently malformed and ten hit a short outage that clears after a few tries. One version wraps each record in a catch-all and carries on: it finishes on time, raises no alert, and saves 20 wrong records. Another stops at the first bad record, number 11, and leaves 90 records unprocessed. A third retries every error three times, including the malformed records, and does 30 attempts more than it needed.
problem: Error handling is not one decision but four: how an error is reported (an exception, a result value, or a code), who is responsible for dealing with it, whether trying again can help, and what the program does to the work in progress. The common mistakes are all ways of skipping that thinking: swallowing the error so the program looks healthy, stopping everything over a recoverable blip, retrying what can never succeed, or logging the same failure at five levels and handling it at none.

howItWorks.title: Fail fast: stop where the problem is
howItWorks.text: Fail fast means detect a broken assumption early and say so at once, close to the cause, instead of passing the bad value onwards. A function that gets an impossible argument throws immediately, rather than returning something that will crash three layers later. The point is diagnosis: the stack trace points at the defect. It does not mean the whole program must die. It means the failing unit stops and reports, and something above decides what that means for the larger job.

howItWorks.title: Pick how the error travels
howItWorks.text: An exception unwinds to a handler and cannot be silently ignored, but it hides the failure path from the type signature. A result value (a success-or-error object, or a pair) shows the failure in the signature and forces the caller to open it. An error code is the cheapest and the easiest to forget. In the sample, all three read the inputs 12, 7, x9, an empty string and 40: the exception stops at item 3, the result collects 2 errors and sums 59, and the unchecked code adds -1 twice and quietly reports 57.

howItWorks.title: Classify before you react
howItWorks.text: A transient error, such as a timeout or a brief outage, can go away if you wait and try again. A permanent error, such as a malformed record, never will. Retrying the first kind is useful, and retrying the second is wasted work. In the simulation, retrying everything makes 149 attempts where classifying makes 119 for the same result. Retries also need to be safe to repeat, which is the idempotency concept, and they need a limit.

howItWorks.title: Handle where you can do something about it
howItWorks.text: A low-level function usually cannot decide what a failed file read means for the user, so it lets the error travel, adding context if it can. A level that can act, by retrying, falling back, telling the user or parking the item, handles it. Handle it once, log it once. Catching at every level, logging, and rethrowing buries the real error in repetition, and catching and returning a default hides it.

howItWorks.title: Match the strategy to how the work is shaped
howItWorks.text: If records are independent, the right unit to fail is the record: park it with its error in a dead-letter queue and continue, which saves 90 of 100. If each record builds on the one before, continuing past a failure corrupts everything after it: dead-lettering then leaves only 10 correct and 80 wrong, and stopping the job is the safe answer. Swallowing is wrong in both cases because nobody is told.

pros: A failure shows up where it happens, so it is found sooner and fixed faster
Telling errors apart (transient, permanent, bug) avoids both wasted retries and unneeded stops
Handling in one place keeps logs clear and behaviour predictable
Setting bad items aside keeps independent work flowing and keeps the evidence
cons: Failing visibly means more alerts and more interruptions, which a team must be ready to act on
Stopping on the first error can leave a batch half done, so the job must be safe to rerun
Result-style handling adds ceremony to every call, and exception-style handling hides paths
Deciding whether an error is transient or permanent is a judgement, and wrong guesses are costly
whenToUse: Fail fast for programming errors, broken invariants and configuration mistakes found at startup
Retry with a limit for timeouts and short outages, when the operation is safe to repeat
Dead-letter and continue for independent items where one bad one should not block the rest
whenNotToUse: Swallowing an error to keep a job green, unless the failure is truly harmless and you say so
Retrying permanent errors, or retrying without a limit and a delay
Stopping a large independent batch on one bad item, when parking it would do
pitfalls: catch (Exception) and carry on: the job succeeds, the data is wrong, and no alert ever fires
Returning a default value for an error, such as 0 or an empty list, which looks like a real answer to the next step
Error codes nobody checks: a -1 flows into a sum, and the total is wrong without a single message
Logging and rethrowing at every level, so one failure appears five times and the real cause is hard to find
Retrying errors that cannot succeed, or non-idempotent actions such as charging a card, so a retry adds a second charge
Failing the whole job on one recoverable blip, so a one-second outage costs a night's work
Dead-lettering records that depend on each other, so everything after the first parked one is computed on missing input
Treating 'let it crash' as 'ignore it': it works where a supervisor restarts the failed part and the work is safe to repeat, and not otherwise

quiz.question: A job sums amounts and uses a parser that returns -1 for a bad value. The caller never checks. What happens with two bad inputs among five?
options: The job stops at the first bad input and reports which one it was.
It reports an error count at the end, because the parser keeps a tally.
It adds -1 for each bad input and reports a wrong sum with no error.
It skips the bad inputs and returns the correct sum of the good ones.
quiz.explanation: An error code that nobody has to check is just a value. The -1 flows into the sum and the total is wrong, silently. An exception or a result type forces the failure to be seen.

quiz.question: A malformed record fails every time it is processed. A job is set to retry every error 3 times. What does this cost compared with retrying only transient errors?
options: Extra attempts for no gain, because the same record fails again each time.
Nothing, because retries are cheap and the record may succeed on the fourth try.
A better chance of fixing the data, because each retry changes the record.
Fewer alerts, because the error is raised once after all the retries.
quiz.explanation: A permanent error will not change between attempts, so every retry is wasted work and delays the alert. Classify errors first: retry timeouts and brief outages, park or reject bad data.

quiz.question: Records in a batch each update a running balance. One record fails and is parked, and the job continues. What is the likely problem?
options: The parked record cannot be read later, because it was removed from the queue.
Every later record is computed from a balance that is missing one record, so they are wrong.
The job slows down, because the dead-letter queue has to be scanned for each record.
Nothing, because parked records are replayed in order when the job ends.
quiz.explanation: Setting a failed item aside is safe only when items are independent. When each depends on the previous result, continuing past a failure builds on missing input, and stopping the job is the safer choice.
